heroIntro: When marital discord surfaces or divorce notices are served in Bangladesh, husbands frequently resort to a dishonest tactic: hastily transferring, selling, or gifting their valuable real estate, residential flats, and commercial shares to trusted family members (such as mothers, brothers, or close friends). The malicious objective is to present themselves as assetless 'paupers' before the Family Court, thereby frustrating the wife's statutory claim to her promised dower (Denmohar) and ongoing child maintenance. Under the Transfer of Property Act 1882, the Family Courts Act 2023, and the Code of Civil Procedure 1898, a wife is legally recognized as an accrued creditor. The law provides decisive legal remedies to set aside sham transfers, freeze husband assets before judgment, and execute recovery against fraudulently conveyed properties.

quickAnswer.title: Can a Wife Challenge Her Husband's Fraudulent Property Transfers in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: Yes. Under Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882, any transfer of immovable property made with the intention to defeat or delay the creditors of the transferor is voidable at the option of any creditor so defeated—and an existing wife holding an accrued dower debt is legally recognized as a creditor. A wife can file a suit in the civil court to declare the fraudulent transfer void under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act 1877. Furthermore, in an ongoing Family Court suit under the Family Courts Act 2023, the wife can immediately file an application for Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38, Rule 5 of the CPC, or seek a temporary injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 to freeze the husband's properties before they can be transferred.
highlights: Wives with accrued dower rights are legally recognized as creditors under Section 53.
Sham gift (Heba) deeds executed to evade dower can be cancelled in civil court.
Family Courts possess authority to order Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38 CPC.
Decrees can be executed by auctioning properties fraudulently conveyed to third-party colluders.

sections.title: 1. The Legal Status of Dower: An Unconditional Statutory Debt in Muslim Law
sections.content:
In Islamic jurisprudence as codified and applied in Bangladesh, dower (Denmohar) is not a customary wedding gift or voluntary gratuity. It is an unconditional statutory debt owed by the husband to the wife arising immediately upon the solemnization of the marriage under the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937.

Dower is categorized into Prompt Dower (Mu'ajjal), which is payable on demand at any time during marriage, and Deferred Dower (Muwajjal), which becomes payable upon dissolution of marriage by divorce or the husband's death. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly established that the wife holds the status of an unsecured creditor in respect of her unpaid dower.

Because the dower liability represents an existing legal obligation, a husband cannot defeat this debt by impoverishing himself through fictitious transactions. When a husband transfers property knowing that divorce is imminent or that the wife has demanded prompt dower, the transfer is presumed under law to be intended to delay and defeat the wife's financial recovery.

sections.title: 2. The Statutory Shield: Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882
sections.content:
The primary statutory weapon against bad-faith debtors attempting to hide real estate is Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 ('Fraudulent Transfer').

Section 53(1) establishes the foundational legal rule: every transfer of immovable property made with intent to defeat or delay the creditors of the transferor shall be voidable at the option of any creditor so defeated or delayed. The section expressly protects bona fide purchasers who acquired property for valuable consideration without notice of the fraudulent intention, but provides zero immunity to gratuitous transferees or colluding family members.

Where a husband gifts or nominally transfers his property to a parent, sibling, or close relative shortly before or immediately after marital breakdown without receiving genuine fair market consideration, the law establishes a strong presumption of fraudulent intent. The affected wife is entitled to file a civil suit to declare the transfer voidable and restore the property to the husband's execution estate.

sections.title: 3. Identifying Sham Transactions: Nominal Heba Deeds and Benami Transfers
sections.content:
Husbands seeking to evade dower almost never sell their property to genuine arms-length third parties; doing so would deprive the family of the asset. Instead, they execute sham transactions within their immediate trusted circle.

The two most common devices deployed are:

  • Fraudulent Heba Deeds (Gifts): The husband executes a registered Heba deed gifting his apartment or land to his mother, brother, or second wife for nominal government registration fees. Crucially, the husband often retains physical possession, collects rental income, and continues residing on the property, proving the gift was a sham without delivery of possession.
  • Benami / Fictitious Sale Deeds: The husband executes a registered Saf Kabala deed to a trusted friend or distant relative showing a fictitious sale price. Banking records reveal that no actual money transferred between the parties, or that cash withdrawn was immediately redeposited into the husband's secret accounts.

Is your husband secretly transferring, gifting, or selling properties to defeat your dower (Denmohar) claim in Bangladesh? Immediate legal action before the properties pass to third parties is vital to freeze the assets. Message our family law advocates on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for confidential guidance.

Courts pierce these colorable transactions by analyzing the proximity of dates between marital disputes and deed registrations, the absence of real consideration, and the retention of physical possession by the husband. For insights on Heba cancellations, review our analysis on Heba deed cancellation laws in Bangladesh.

sections.title: 4. Freezing Assets Fast: Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC
sections.content:
When a wife initiates a suit for recovery of dower and maintenance in the Family Court under the Family Courts Act 2023, waiting for the final judgment (which may take 12 to 24 months) creates an acute risk that the husband will dispose of all immovable properties during the trial.

To eliminate this threat, the wife's advocate must immediately file an emergency application for Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38, Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The application demonstrates that the defendant husband, with intent to obstruct or delay the execution of any decree that may be passed against him, is about to dispose of the whole or part of his property.

The Family Court issues a notice commanding the husband to either furnish sufficient financial security (such as a bank guarantee) to satisfy the dower claim or appear and show cause why his properties should not be attached. If the husband fails to furnish security, the court issues a formal attachment order. A copy of the attachment order is transmitted to the relevant Sub-Registry Office and AC Land office, legally prohibiting any deed registration or mutation pending final trial.

sections.title: 5. Temporary Injunctions under Order 39: Restraining Immovable Transfers
sections.content:
In addition to attachment before judgment, an application for a temporary injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the CPC provides vital interim protection. While an attachment creates an official government encumbrance, an injunction directly restrains the husband personaliter.

To obtain an injunction, the wife must establish the three classic equitable tests: a prima facie case (proven by the registered Nikahnama showing unpaid dower), irreparable financial injury if the husband becomes assetless, and the balance of convenience lying in favor of preserving the status quo.

The court passes an ad-interim or temporary injunction restraining the husband, his agents, and nominees from selling, transferring, gifting, mortgaging, or changing the physical character of the specified properties. Disobedience of an injunction order exposes the husband to civil detention under Order 39, Rule 2A CPC, providing powerful leverage to preserve assets.

sections.title: 6. Summary Matrix: Asset Protection Remedies, Prerequisites & Fora
sections.content:
Wives facing fraudulent asset dissipation can evaluate the operational distinctions between emergency protective mechanisms in the following comparative matrix:

Legal Remedy Governing Statute / Rule Prerequisites for Relief Effect on Husband's Property
Attachment Before Judgment Order 38 Rule 5 CPC Proof of attempt to dispose of property to defeat decree Registry encumbrance; property cannot be sold or mortgaged
Temporary Injunction Order 39 Rules 1 & 2 CPC Prima facie title, balance of convenience, irreparable injury Restrains husband from executing deeds; violation triggers jail

Execution by Auction Sale Family Courts Act & Order 21 CPC Final decree for unpaid dower and failure to satisfy debt Court auctions attached properties to pay dower to wife

sections.title: 7. Setting Aside Fraudulent Deeds: Section 39 Specific Relief Act Lawsuits
sections.content:
If the wife discovers that the husband has already registered a sham Heba deed or fictitious sale deed before she could obtain an injunction, all hope is not lost. The transaction can be directly annulled through a declaratory title suit.

The wife, as an aggrieved creditor, files a suit under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act 1877 read with Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 in the competent Assistant Judge or Joint District Judge Court. The plaint impleads both the husband and the colluding transferee (e.g., the mother-in-law or brother-in-law), detailing that the transfer was nominal, lacked consideration, and was engineered solely to defeat the accrued dower debt.

Upon evaluating the evidence and finding that the transfer was fraudulent, the civil court enters a decree adjudging the deed void, commands the Sub-Registry Office to make an entry of cancellation in the official Balam Boi records, and restores title to the husband's name, rendering the asset available for execution. sections.title: 8. Illustrative Scenario: Recovering 30 Lakh BDT Dower Against a Sham Heba Deed
sections.content:
To understand how this dual litigation strategy operates in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A corporate director in Dhanmondi, Dhaka, entered into a registered Nikahnama stipulating a dower of 30 Lakh BDT. After eight years of marriage, the husband served a notice of divorce under Section 7 of the MFLO. Simultaneously, he executed a registered Heba deed gifting his primary asset—a 4-story commercial building in Mirpur valued at 4 Crore BDT—exclusively to his elderly mother, while claiming before the Family Court that he had zero immovable property and could only afford 5,000 BDT monthly maintenance.

The wife engaged a Supreme Court family advocate. The advocate immediately obtained a certified copy of the Heba deed from the Sub-Registry Office, confirming that the transfer occurred exactly fourteen days after the divorce notice was issued. The legal team filed a suit in the Family Court for recovery of the 30 Lakh BDT dower, accompanied by an Order 38 Rule 5 application for attachment before judgment over the Mirpur property.

Concurrently, the advocate filed a suit under Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act and Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act to cancel the sham Heba deed. The court observed that the mother paid zero consideration, the husband continued collecting commercial rents, and the transfer was executed solely to defeat the wife's debt. The court cancelled the Heba deed, decreed the full 30 Lakh BDT dower, and attached the commercial building. Confronted with an impending court auction, the husband satisfied the entire dower decree in cash.

sections.title: 9. Essential Evidentiary Checklist for Wives Facing Asset Dissipation
sections.content:
Wives suspecting that their husbands are preparing to conceal assets should take immediate, proactive legal steps to preserve evidence:

  • Procure Certified Nikahnama & Kazi Records: Obtain certified copies of the registered Kabinnama detailing the prompt and deferred dower figures and any property pledged as dower.
  • Document Real Estate Identifiers: Secure plot numbers, Mouza names, Khatian numbers, and Sub-Registry details of all lands, apartments, and commercial holdings owned by the husband.
  • Track Corporate & Banking Assets: Identify company names, directorship records from the RJSC, bank branches, and vehicle registration numbers registered in the husband's name.
  • Act Before Deeds Are Registered: File an emergency Family Court petition seeking Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC at the very first indication of marital breakdown.
  • Challenge Sub-Registry Transfers Immediately: If a deed is executed, obtain certified copies (Nokol) immediately and file a Section 53 cancellation suit before third-party rights intervene.

faqs.question: Can a husband legally gift all his property to his mother to avoid paying dower?
faqs.answer: No. Under Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882, transfers made with intent to defeat or delay creditors (including a wife owed dower) are voidable. A court can declare the gift deed fraudulent and set it aside.

faqs.question: Is a wife considered a creditor of her husband under Bangladeshi law?
faqs.answer: Yes. Islamic law and Bangladeshi judicial precedents establish that unpaid dower (Denmohar) is an unconditional debt, placing the wife in the legal position of a creditor against her husband's estate.

faqs.question: What is Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC?
faqs.answer: Attachment Before Judgment is an emergency court order that freezes the defendant's immovable properties during an ongoing trial, preventing them from selling or transferring assets to evade satisfying a future decree.

faqs.question: Can the Family Court auction a husband's property to pay unpaid dower?
faqs.answer: Yes. In execution proceedings under the Family Courts Act 2023 and Order 21 CPC, if the husband fails to pay the decreed dower, the court can seize, attach, and auction his properties to satisfy the debt.

faqs.question: What happens if a husband transfers land to a stranger for nominal value?
faqs.answer: If the transfer was made to a colluding third party for nominal or fictitious consideration with notice of the dispute, it can be cancelled under Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act and Section 39 Specific Relief Act.

faqs.question: Can a wife freeze her husband's bank accounts for dower recovery?
faqs.answer: Yes. A wife can apply to the Family Court or High Court to attach the husband's commercial bank accounts, salary, and company dividends to secure payment of her dower and child maintenance.

faqs.question: What should I do if my husband threatens to divorce me without giving my dower?
faqs.answer: Immediately retain counsel to file a Family Court suit for recovery of prompt dower and maintenance, accompanied by an Order 38 Rule 5 petition to attach his real estate before divorce notices take effect.

faqs.question: Can an overseas Bangladeshi wife sue her husband for dower from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. An overseas wife can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission, authorizing an advocate in Dhaka to file the suit and attach properties without returning to Bangladesh.
